lesson_title: Reading the Stats Sheet: Analysing Partnership Statements
hook_text: The shop made R528 000. Great year or lazy year? The results board knows.
clip_script: No coach watches every race an athlete has ever run. She reads the results board — personal bests, split times. Small numbers standing in for a big performance. That is what analysis does to a business. Profitability is the personal-best column: out of every hundred rand of sales, thirty-seven and a half survive paying for the goods, and a touch over eighteen reach the owners. Then the tempo section: one rand runs a lap — becomes a tin of paint, waits 46 days on the shelf, becomes a customer's promise, waits 15 days more, crosses the line as cash. Meanwhile the supplier is paid at day 25, so from day 25 to day 61 the shop runs the lap on its own money. Then the verdict questions. Can it survive? More than four times cover on the bills — safe, maybe too safe, with R134 000 asleep in the bank. Was it worth it? The partners' money earned 62,4 percent; the bank would have paid nine. But here is the coach's first rule, the whole subject in one line: a number means nothing alone. Every number needs its next-to — last year, the plan, the rival. No comparison, no meaning. Comparison, cause, advice — that is how the marks are scored.
visual_style: A coach's clipboard morphing into financial statements, stat tiles flipping like a stadium results board, a rand coin running laps around shelf, promise and bank icons with day-counters ticking; energetic track-side palette.
pacing: Quick stat flips, a steady lap sequence with counters, then a decisive verdict beat.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and hand down your own verdict — four beats per comment.
